name: Capryloyl salicylic acid (LHA)

card.summary: A fat-soluble salicylic acid derivative used in cosmetic exfoliants and acne products to unclog pores and smooth skin texture.
card.note: A 2024 cosmetic ingredient review found data insufficient to conclude on safety.

quick.overview:
Capryloyl salicylic acid, called LHA, is a lipophilic derivative of salicylic acid found in some skincare products, including La Roche-Posay lines. Because it is oil-soluble, it is used to exfoliate and clear pores.

The appearance payoff is clearer, smoother skin with fewer clogged pores. A controlled clinical trial from 2002 examined topical LHA as a comedolytic (pore-clearing) agent for acne.
quick.how: It is applied as a leave-on or rinse-off cosmetic exfoliant within a skincare routine, often alongside moisturiser and sunscreen.
quick.risks: The Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel reassessed it in 2024 and concluded the available data are insufficient to determine safety under intended cosmetic conditions of use. Irritation is possible, as with other exfoliants.

lead: Capryloyl salicylic acid, marketed as LHA (beta-lipohydroxy acid), is a salicylic acid derivative with an added fatty chain that makes it lipophilic, meaning it dissolves in oils rather than water. It appears in cosmetic skin conditioners and acne-oriented products, including lines sold by La Roche-Posay.[1][4]

People use it for the same visible goals as other exfoliating acids: fewer blackheads and clogged pores, a smoother surface and a clearer-looking complexion. The chain proposed by makers and users is that an oil-soluble acid can work inside the sebum-filled pore, loosening the plug of shed skin cells and oil that forms a comedone.[3][5]

A controlled clinical trial published in 2002 by G. E. Pierard and A. Rougier studied topical LHA as a comedolytic (pore-clearing) agent in acne.[2] In 2024 the Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety reassessed the ingredient and concluded that the available data were insufficient to determine safety under intended cosmetic conditions of use.[1]

angle.text: LHA is used to exfoliate and clear pores, targeting blackheads and rough texture.

infobox: Lipophilic (oil-soluble) fatty-chain derivative of salicylic acid
Leave-on and rinse-off exfoliants, acne-oriented cleansers and treatments

paras: Salicylic acid is a beta hydroxy acid; in cosmetics the term beta hydroxy acid refers specifically to salicylic acid.[4] Wikipedia notes that salicylic acid makes epidermal cells slough off more readily, which keeps pores from clogging, and lists acne among the conditions it is used for in skincare products.[3] Capryloyl salicylic acid is a derivative in which a fatty (capryloyl) group is attached, and this is the feature behind the name beta-lipohydroxy acid.[1][2]

The cosmetic ingredient review panel lists its function as skin conditioning.[1] Brands market it as a gentler, oil-soluble alternative or complement to plain salicylic acid within acne-prone and blemish-care ranges.

sections.h: How it is used to improve appearance
paras: Users apply LHA products as part of a regular routine, typically a cleanser, exfoliating lotion or serum followed by moisturiser and sunscreen. The visible aims are fewer blackheads and whiteheads, less surface roughness, and a more even-looking texture.

Acne is diagnosed by the presence of comedones, the clogged follicles seen as blackheads and whiteheads, and acne can leave marks and affect self-confidence.[5] Exfoliating acids that reduce comedones are therefore a common part of acne-oriented routines. The Wikipedia acne article describes salicylic acid as opening obstructed pores and promoting shedding of skin cells, and notes that dry skin is its most common side effect.[5]

The published human work on topical LHA centres on a 2002 controlled clinical trial report in the European Journal of Dermatology, authored by Pierard and Rougier and titled as a study of LHA as a new comedolytic agent in acne.[2] Cosmetic-industry safety review followed later, with the Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety publishing its reassessment online in March 2024.[1]

The 2024 panel, whose authors include Wilbur Johnson Jr and Wilma Bergfeld, described the ingredient's function as skin conditioning and concluded the available data were insufficient to determine that it is safe under intended conditions of use in cosmetic formulations.[1] That is a statement about the size of the data set rather than a report of specific harms.

Related exfoliants carry known effects: salicylic acid's most common side effect is dryness, and the EU restricts salicylic acid by concentration in cosmetics and in products for young children.[3][5] Wikipedia's salicylic acid article also describes salicylic acid as an EU category 2 reproductive toxicant, a classification applying to the parent compound.[3]

A controlled clinical trial of topical LHA as a comedolytic acne agent was published in 2002 by Pierard and Rougier; the PubMed record carries no abstract, so detailed design and results are not available from it.[2] Few other published human trials are available. The 2024 safety review is a toxicological assessment rather than an efficacy trial.[1]

timeline.event: Controlled clinical trial of topical LHA in acne published in the European Journal of Dermatology by Pierard and Rougier.[2]
Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety publishes its reassessment of capryloyl salicylic acid, finding data insufficient to determine safety.[1]
